title: Last-Write-Wins Memory: Isolating Deterministic Overwrite Semantics for Long-Context Conflict Resolution

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to resolve conflicting fact versions in LLM agent memory at the source rather than relying on the language model during reasoning. None of the prior papers explicitly address this purpose. While papers like [2] and [7] discuss memory conflicts and reasoning in LLM agents, they focus on analyzing or mitigating the impact of conflicts during reasoning, rather than resolving conflicts at the memory source itself. Therefore, no prior paper shares this specific objective.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, LWW-KO, applies last-write-wins deterministic overwrite semantics to structured knowledge objects, filtering stale fact versions before retrieval. Papers [13], [19], [26], and [30] discuss conflict resolution or versioning in distributed systems and databases, including optimistic replication and conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs). These works describe mechanisms for resolving conflicts using deterministic rules, including last-write-wins semantics ([13], [19]) and conflict-free merging ([26], [30]). While these papers focus on distributed systems or databases rather than LLM memory, the underlying primitive of deterministic overwrite semantics for conflict resolution is substantively equivalent across domains.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses the FactConsolidation benchmark to measure multi-hop and single-hop accuracy improvements. Papers [4], [12], and [16] describe evaluation designs for memory systems in LLM agents, including benchmarks for long-term memory, multi-hop recall, and reasoning tasks. While the specific benchmark instance (FactConsolidation) is new, the evaluation design — measuring multi-hop and single-hop accuracy on memory-augmented LLM tasks — is covered by these prior works. For example, [4] and [12] evaluate memory systems on multi-hop recall and long-context question answering tasks, which share the same design logic.

### Domain
The domain is LLM agent long-term memory and conflict resolution. Papers [1], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [11], [12], [14], [15], and [16] all operate in the general application area of LLM agent memory systems, including long-term memory and conflict resolution. While this contribution targets a specific sub-problem (conflict resolution at the memory source), the broader domain of LLM agent memory is well-covered by prior work.
